title: Classifying bipartite entanglement
lede: Every idea used to sort two-party states: what counts as a party, what operations are free, what tests can see, what a state can do, and how much of it there is.

nodes.label: Bipartite entanglement
nodes.title: Classifying bipartite entanglement
nodes.statement: There is no single classification of two-party entanglement. Each idea here sorts states by a different question: what are the parties, what can they do, what can a test see, what can the state be used for, and how much of it is there? This map gathers those ideas and shows how they cut across one another.

nodes.label: What counts as a party
nodes.title: What counts as a party
nodes.statement: Before any state can be classified, the system has to be split in two. That split is usually taken for granted, but it is a choice, and it is not always a tensor product of two Hilbert spaces.

nodes.label: Subsystems come from observables
nodes.title: A tensor product structure is induced by accessible observables
nodes.statement: Which subsystems exist depends on which observables can be controlled and measured, so entanglement is relative to that choice rather than a property of a state vector alone.

nodes.label: Fermions: Slater rank
nodes.title: Slater rank replaces Schmidt rank for two fermions
nodes.statement: Two-fermion pure states have a Slater decomposition and a Slater rank, analogous to the Schmidt decomposition and rank. Mixed states are then sorted by their Slater number, the smallest Slater rank needed to build them.

nodes.label: Identical particles: modes or particles
nodes.title: Mode entanglement and particle entanglement differ
nodes.statement: With indistinguishable particles, entanglement can be assigned to modes or restricted to what parties can actually extract. The operational quantity is bounded by the mode-occupation value, and a single particle shared across two modes has none of it.

nodes.label: Infinite dimensions
nodes.title: Infinite-dimensional systems need more careful definitions
nodes.statement: In infinite dimensions, states with infinite entropy of entanglement are trace-norm dense, so every product state has arbitrarily entangled neighbours. A bound on mean energy restores sensible behaviour.

nodes.label: Field theory: no factorisation
nodes.title: In quantum field theory, regions do not factorise
nodes.statement: Entanglement here is a property of the algebra of observables, not only of states. Regions and their complements do not give a tensor product of two Hilbert spaces, so entropy needs more careful treatment.

nodes.label: Tensor versus commuting models
nodes.title: Tensor-product and commuting-operator correlations differ
nodes.statement: Separation can be modelled by a tensor product or by commuting operators on one space. MIP* = RE implies the two give different correlation sets, a negative answer to Tsirelson's problem.

nodes.label: Pure states: Schmidt data
nodes.title: Pure states are classified by their Schmidt coefficients
nodes.statement: A bipartite pure state is summarised by its Schmidt coefficients. Each notion of equivalence reads a different amount from that list: all of it, its length, its majorization order, or only its entropy.

nodes.label: LU: the full Schmidt list
nodes.title: Local unitaries preserve exactly the Schmidt coefficients
nodes.statement: Two bipartite pure states are related by local unitaries exactly when they have the same Schmidt coefficients. This is the finest classification on the page.

nodes.label: SLOCC: Schmidt rank
nodes.title: Stochastic LOCC classes are labelled by Schmidt rank
nodes.statement: If conversion only has to succeed with non-zero probability, a pure state can reach another exactly when its Schmidt rank is at least as large. Mutual convertibility therefore means equal rank.

nodes.label: LOCC: majorization order
nodes.title: Deterministic LOCC gives a partial order
nodes.statement: With LOCC and certainty required, Schmidt coefficients are compared by majorization. The result is an order, not a list of classes.

nodes.label: Nielsen's theorem
nodes.title: Majorization decides deterministic pure state conversion
nodes.statement: A pure state converts to another by LOCC exactly when its Schmidt coefficients are majorized by those of the target.

nodes.label: Incomparable states
nodes.title: Some pure states cannot be converted in either direction
nodes.statement: Majorization is only a partial order, so there are pairs of states neither of which can deterministically reach the other. No single number can capture single-copy convertibility.

nodes.label: Vidal's conversion probability
nodes.title: A finite set of monotones gives the optimal conversion probability
nodes.statement: When conversion cannot be certain, its best probability is set by a finite family of monotones built from the Schmidt coefficients. These quantify the entanglement of a single copy.

nodes.label: With catalysts
nodes.title: Catalysts coarsen the order
nodes.statement: Allowing an entangled state that is returned at the end enlarges what is reachable. The order relaxes in stages, ending at a single number.

nodes.label: Trumping
nodes.title: Catalysts enable conversions majorization forbids
nodes.statement: Some transformations ruled out by Nielsen's theorem become possible with a catalyst that is recovered intact. The resulting relation between Schmidt vectors is called trumping.

nodes.label: Trumping fully characterised
nodes.title: Explicit inequalities decide the trumping relation
nodes.statement: Turgut and Klimesh independently gave complete families of inequalities that decide whether one Schmidt vector can trump another.

nodes.label: Correlated: entropy decides
nodes.title: With correlated catalysts, entropy alone decides conversion
nodes.statement: If the catalyst may end up correlated with the system, entanglement entropy completely characterises pure state transformations, even for a single copy.

nodes.label: Many copies: entropy only
nodes.title: Asymptotically, entropy is the only invariant
nodes.statement: With many copies, pure states convert reversibly at a rate set by the entropy of the reduced state. All the structure of the Schmidt list collapses to one number.

nodes.label: Shape of the state space
nodes.title: The geometry of mixed states
nodes.statement: Mixed states form a convex body with the separable states inside it. Classifying a state can mean locating it in that body: by the sets it belongs to, its orbit under local operations, or its distance from the boundary.

nodes.label: Separable states form a convex set
nodes.title: The separable states are a convex set
nodes.statement: Mixtures of product states are closed under further mixing, so any entangled state can be separated from the set by a hyperplane. That geometric fact is what makes entanglement witnesses exist.

nodes.label: How large is the separable set?
nodes.title: How large is the separable set?
nodes.statement: The separable set has non-zero volume, but how much of state space it fills depends strongly on dimension and on how states are drawn.

nodes.label: Positive volume
nodes.title: The separable states have positive volume
nodes.statement: Separable states are not a negligible set: they occupy a positive fraction of the state space in any finite dimension.

nodes.label: Separable ball
nodes.title: A ball of separable states surrounds the maximally mixed state
nodes.statement: All states close enough to the maximally mixed state are separable. Gurvits and Barnum bound the largest such ball.

nodes.label: Random states: sharp threshold
nodes.title: Random induced states change from entangled to separable sharply
nodes.statement: For a random state on two d-dimensional systems, obtained by tracing out an environment of dimension s, there is a sharp threshold of order roughly d³. Below it the state is very probably entangled, above it very probably separable.

nodes.label: Separable from the spectrum
nodes.title: What can the eigenvalues alone decide?
nodes.statement: Some states are separable however they are rotated globally. For those, the eigenvalues are enough, and no entangling unitary can help.

nodes.label: Absolutely separable states
nodes.title: Absolutely separable states stay separable under every global unitary
nodes.statement: Kuś and Życzkowski defined this class, in which every state with the same spectrum is separable.

nodes.label: Absolutely PPT from spectrum
nodes.title: Absolutely PPT states have a spectral characterisation
nodes.statement: Hildebrand showed that whether every rotation of a state remains PPT can be decided from its eigenvalues, using a finite set of linear matrix inequalities.

nodes.label: Qubit-qudit case settled
nodes.title: For qubit-qudit systems, absolutely separable equals absolutely PPT
nodes.statement: In 2×n systems, the two spectral classes coincide, so the question is answered by a simple condition on the eigenvalues.

nodes.label: Is absolutely PPT always separable?
nodes.title: Does absolutely PPT imply absolutely separable in every dimension?
nodes.statement: The two sets coincide in the qubit-qudit case, and absolutely separable states are always absolutely PPT. Whether the converse holds generally is the question.
nodes.unknown: The general equivalence has not been proved or refuted. Arunachalam, Johnston and Russo show that a wide range of witnesses and positive maps cannot separate the two sets.

nodes.label: Local orbits and normal forms
nodes.title: Sorting mixed states by local orbits and normal forms
nodes.statement: Two mixed states count as the same if local operations relate them. Invariants and normal forms label these orbits, in place of the Schmidt list that pure states enjoy.

nodes.label: Local orbit dimensions
nodes.title: Local orbits can differ in dimension
nodes.statement: Explicit methods compute the dimension of the local orbit of any mixed state, which characterises the set of effectively different states.

nodes.label: Local unitary invariants
nodes.title: Polynomial invariants label local unitary classes
nodes.statement: Local unitary classes of mixed states can be separated by polynomial invariants of the density matrix. Makhlin gave a full set for mixed states of two qubits.

nodes.label: Filtering normal form
nodes.title: Local filtering brings states to a normal form
nodes.statement: Invertible local filters generalise the singular value decomposition to mixed states. For two qubits this is a Lorentz singular value decomposition, which gives a concrete analysis of separability.

nodes.label: Hilbert-Schmidt picture of 2×2
nodes.title: A complete picture of two-qubit states with maximally mixed subsystems
nodes.statement: Written in the Hilbert-Schmidt basis, two-qubit states with maximally disordered subsystems admit a complete characterisation of which are inseparable.

nodes.label: Best separable approximation
nodes.title: Every state splits into a separable part and an entangled remainder
nodes.statement: A state can be decomposed with the largest possible separable weight, leaving an entangled remainder. This gives a way to compare states by how much separable part they contain.

nodes.label: Schmidt-number ladder
nodes.title: The Schmidt number sorts mixed states into nested sets
nodes.statement: Schmidt rank extends to mixed states as a ladder of nested convex sets, in which separable states are only the first rung.

nodes.label: Schmidt number
nodes.title: The Schmidt number extends rank to mixed states
nodes.statement: A mixed state's Schmidt number is the smallest k such that it can be built from pure states of Schmidt rank at most k, minimised over all decompositions. Separable states have Schmidt number 1.

nodes.label: k-positive maps detect it
nodes.title: k-positive maps detect Schmidt number
nodes.statement: A state has Schmidt number at most k exactly when k-positive maps send it to a positive operator. This extends the positive-map test for separability up the ladder.

nodes.label: Schmidt-number witnesses
nodes.title: Witnesses can certify a lower bound on Schmidt number
nodes.statement: Sanpera, Bruß and Lewenstein give a canonical form for Schmidt-number witnesses, along with methods to optimise them.

nodes.label: Two-qutrit PPT: Schmidt number 2
nodes.title: Two-qutrit PPT states have Schmidt number at most 2
nodes.statement: Sanpera, Bruß and Lewenstein gave strong evidence for this. Yang, Leung and Tang, and independently Choi, proved that every 2-positive map from M3 to M3 is decomposable, which is the dual statement.

nodes.label: Separability tests
nodes.title: What separability tests can see
nodes.statement: Every test divides states into those it flags and those it misses, so the tests themselves classify states. Deciding separability exactly is NP-hard, so the useful question is which test sees which states.

nodes.label: Positive maps
nodes.title: Positive maps classify entanglement by what they can detect
nodes.statement: A positive but not completely positive map applied to one party can turn an entangled state into something with a negative eigenvalue. The structure of these maps mirrors the structure of entanglement.

nodes.label: All positive maps: complete
nodes.title: Positive maps collectively decide separability
nodes.statement: A state is separable exactly when it stays positive under every positive map applied to one party. The test is complete, but no general description of all positive maps exists.

nodes.label: Transpose: the PPT test
nodes.title: The transpose gives the partial transpose test
nodes.statement: The transpose is the most familiar positive map. It splits states into PPT and NPT, and PPT states cannot be distilled. Whether every NPT state can be is still open.

nodes.label: Reduction criterion
nodes.title: The reduction criterion ties detection to distillation
nodes.statement: The reduction map gives a separability test, and a state that violates it can be distilled. Cerf, Adami and Gingrich reached the same criterion through a conditional operator.

nodes.label: Decomposable maps miss PPT states
nodes.title: Decomposable maps cannot detect PPT entanglement
nodes.statement: A decomposable map adds nothing beyond the partial transpose. Detecting PPT entangled states requires an indecomposable map, the first example of which came from Choi. In 2×2 and 2×3, every positive map is decomposable.

nodes.label: Indecomposable constructions
nodes.title: Families of indecomposable maps reveal bound entanglement
nodes.statement: Explicit families of non-decomposable positive maps detect PPT entangled states in even dimensions and in 2^N×2^N systems. Each family reveals a different slice of them.

nodes.label: Optimal witnesses
nodes.title: Witnesses can be optimised against the separable set
nodes.statement: Lewenstein and coauthors give necessary and sufficient conditions for a witness to be optimal. They construct non-decomposable witnesses from edge states, which ties the structure of witnesses to that of PPT entanglement.

nodes.label: Structure of all positive maps
nodes.title: What is the general structure of positive maps?
nodes.statement: A full description of positive maps would solve the separability problem through the Horodecki criterion, so the two questions are closely tied.
nodes.unknown: No general characterisation of positive maps is known in dimensions where indecomposable maps exist. Since deciding separability is NP-hard, a simple one is not expected.

nodes.label: Rearrangements and correlations
nodes.title: Tests from rearranged matrices and correlations
nodes.statement: A second family of tests needs no positive map. It bounds a norm or a covariance that separable states cannot exceed, and often catches PPT entangled states.

nodes.label: Realignment (CCNR)
nodes.title: The computable cross norm and realignment criterion
nodes.statement: Realigning the density matrix and summing its singular values gives a quantity at most 1 on separable states.

nodes.label: Covariance matrices
nodes.title: Covariance matrices unify several criteria
nodes.statement: Conditions on covariance matrices of local observables give strong criteria that detect many bound entangled states, are necessary and sufficient for two qubits, and clarify how earlier criteria are related.

nodes.label: Local uncertainty relations
nodes.title: Violating local uncertainty relations signals entanglement
nodes.statement: Separable states inherit uncertainty bounds from their local parts. Hofmann and Takeuchi show that violating such a sum bound is a signature of entanglement.

nodes.label: Bloch correlation tensor
nodes.title: The correlation tensor gives a separability condition
nodes.statement: Writing a state in terms of local generators gives a correlation tensor. Bounding its norm yields separability conditions and lower bounds on concurrence.

nodes.label: Global versus local disorder
nodes.title: Tests comparing global and local disorder
nodes.statement: Separable states cannot be more ordered globally than locally. Entropy and majorization turn that intuition into tests.

nodes.label: Entropic criteria
nodes.title: Negative conditional entropy implies entanglement
nodes.statement: Inseparability is linked to conditional α-entropy inequalities: a state more disordered locally than globally cannot be separable.

nodes.label: Majorization criterion
nodes.title: Separable states are more disordered globally than locally
nodes.statement: For a separable state, the global spectrum is majorized by each local spectrum. This is stronger than the entropy inequality alone.

nodes.label: Range and product vectors
nodes.title: Tests based on range, rank and product vectors
nodes.statement: A separable state's range is spanned by product vectors whose local conjugates span the range of its partial transpose. Rank and range thus classify PPT states that spectral tests cannot reach.

nodes.label: Range criterion
nodes.title: The range criterion detects PPT entangled states
nodes.statement: The range condition gave the first explicit PPT entangled states, in 3×3 and 2×4.

nodes.label: Unextendible product bases
nodes.title: Unextendible product bases build bound entangled states
nodes.statement: A set of orthogonal product vectors with no further product vector orthogonal to it leaves a complement containing no product states. The normalised projector onto that complement is bound entangled.

nodes.label: Low rank: PPT suffices
nodes.title: Low-rank PPT states are separable
nodes.statement: For an M×N state with M ≤ N and rank at most N, PPT is necessary and sufficient for separability, so there are no rank-3 PPT entangled states.

nodes.label: Edge states
nodes.title: Edge states sit at the boundary of PPT entanglement
nodes.statement: An edge state is a PPT entangled state from which no product vector can be subtracted while staying PPT. Lewenstein and coauthors use them to build optimal witnesses.

nodes.label: Rank-four qutrit states
nodes.title: Two-qutrit rank-four PPT entangled states all come from UPBs
nodes.statement: Every two-qutrit PPT entangled state of rank four can be built from an unextendible product basis. Chen and Đoković also determine the closure of this set.

nodes.label: Extensions and complexity
nodes.title: Extendibility, and the limits of efficient testing
nodes.statement: Entanglement cannot be freely shared. Asking how widely a state can be extended yields a complete test, along with a measure of how hard the problem is.

nodes.label: Symmetric-extension hierarchy
nodes.title: A hierarchy of symmetric extensions detects all entanglement
nodes.statement: Separable states have symmetric extensions at every level. An entangled state fails at some finite level, and each level is a semidefinite program.

nodes.label: Monogamy bounds extension
nodes.title: Monogamy limits how far correlations can be shared
nodes.statement: Koashi and Winter give an identity trading entanglement with one party against classical correlation with another, from which rigorous monogamy relations follow.

nodes.label: NP-hardness
nodes.title: No efficient complete test is expected
nodes.statement: Deciding separability is NP-hard, even within an inverse polynomial distance of the separable set. Any complete classification by easy tests is therefore not expected unless P = NP.

nodes.label: Partial transpose moments
nodes.title: Moments of the partial transpose can be measured directly
nodes.statement: Randomised local measurements estimate moments of the partial transpose without full tomography. Yu, Imai and Gühne find the optimal entanglement certification these moments allow.

nodes.label: Distillability classes
nodes.title: Free and bound entanglement
nodes.statement: Can a state be turned back into pure entangled pairs? This operational question divides entangled states into free and bound, and leaves one major boundary unsettled.

nodes.label: Free entanglement
nodes.title: Distillable states can be purified into singlets
nodes.statement: Given many sufficiently pure noisy pairs, LOCC can extract fewer pairs of arbitrarily high fidelity. This defines the free entangled class.

nodes.label: Two qubits: all free
nodes.title: Every entangled two-qubit state is distillable
nodes.statement: In the smallest case, the classes coincide: entangled and free mean the same thing.

nodes.label: PPT entangled: bound
nodes.title: PPT entangled states cannot be distilled
nodes.statement: A distillable state must violate the partial transpose test. PPT entangled states therefore form a class of bound entanglement.

nodes.label: The NPT boundary
nodes.title: Is every NPT state distillable?
nodes.statement: Bound entanglement is known on the PPT side. Whether it also exists on the NPT side is the central open question of this classification.

nodes.label: Reduces to Werner states
nodes.title: The question reduces to Werner states
nodes.statement: Local filtering and twirling take any NPT state to an NPT Werner state. If all NPT Werner states are distillable, then so are all NPT states.

nodes.label: Do NPT bound states exist?
nodes.title: Do bound entangled states with a negative partial transpose exist?
nodes.statement: Every distillable state is NPT. Evidence going back to 1999 suggests the converse may fail in dimensions above 2×2, with Werner states as the key test family.
nodes.unknown: The question remains listed among the five open problems of Horodecki, Rudnicki and Życzkowski, and was still called long-standing in 2024. A 2006 preprint claimed existence, but later work continues to treat the question as open.

nodes.label: Two copies of NPT Werner fail
nodes.title: NPT Werner states are two-copy undistillable in every dimension
nodes.statement: A July 2026 preprint proves a partial-trace matrix inequality and uses it to claim two-copy undistillability of NPT Werner states in arbitrary local dimension.
nodes.unknown: No independent confirmation had been found by the check date. Even if correct, it covers two copies, while NPT bound entanglement requires every number of copies.

nodes.label: PPT-preserving ops distil all NPT
nodes.title: PPT-preserving channels distil every NPT state
nodes.statement: All NPT states are distillable under channels that preserve the partial transpose's positivity. The open question therefore turns on the gap between separable and PPT-preserving operations.

nodes.label: Hierarchy of correlations
nodes.title: Sorting states by the correlations they support
nodes.statement: Entanglement is one rung in a ladder of correlations, with discord below it and steering and Bell nonlocality above. The picture changes once local filtering, many copies or side resources are allowed.

nodes.label: Discord: below entanglement
nodes.title: Quantum discord separates classical from quantum correlation
nodes.statement: Discord compares two forms of mutual information that agree classically. Its vanishing is a stricter condition than separability, so some separable states still carry it.

nodes.label: Steering is strictly between
nodes.title: Steering lies strictly between entanglement and Bell nonlocality
nodes.statement: Wiseman, Jones and Doherty define steering operationally. Bell nonlocal states are steerable and steerable states are entangled, and neither inclusion can be reversed.

nodes.label: Entangled yet local?
nodes.title: Can entangled states have a local model?
nodes.statement: Entangled states need not violate a Bell inequality directly. What looks local can however become nonlocal once more resources are allowed.

nodes.label: Local models exist
nodes.title: Some entangled states admit a local hidden-variable model
nodes.statement: Werner built a model for projective measurements on some entangled states. Barrett extended the conclusion to general POVM measurements.

nodes.label: Hidden nonlocality
nodes.title: Local filtering can reveal hidden nonlocality
nodes.statement: Popescu showed that sequential measurements, with a local filter first, can reveal Bell nonlocality in states that have a local model for direct measurements.

nodes.label: Superactivation of nonlocality
nodes.title: Copies of a local state can violate a Bell inequality
nodes.statement: Palazuelos showed that tensoring a local state with itself can produce a Bell violation, so nonlocality is not fixed by the behaviour of a single copy.

nodes.label: Semi-quantum games: all nonlocal
nodes.title: All entangled states are nonlocal in semi-quantum games
nodes.statement: Buscemi shows that a suitable class of nonlocal games, in which referees ask quantum questions, witnesses every entangled state. So what counts as nonlocal depends on the test.

nodes.label: Asymptotic CHSH = distillable
nodes.title: Asymptotic CHSH violation is equivalent to distillability
nodes.statement: If local processing over arbitrarily many copies is allowed, violating CHSH is the same as being distillable. Bound entangled states do not violate it in this asymptotic sense.

nodes.label: Peres conjectures
nodes.title: Do nonlocality and bound entanglement exclude each other?
nodes.statement: Peres conjectured that PPT states would admit local models. Both the original form and its steering-based strengthening were later disproved.

nodes.label: PPT states are Bell-local
nodes.title: Bound entangled states never violate a Bell inequality
nodes.statement: False. Vértesi and Brunner found a bound entangled state violating a Bell inequality, so nonlocality implies neither distillability nor a negative partial transpose.

nodes.label: PPT states can't steer
nodes.title: Bound entangled states can never be used for steering
nodes.statement: False. Moroder and coauthors gave bound entangled states that show steering, a counterexample to the stronger Peres conjecture.

nodes.label: Usefulness for tasks
nodes.title: Sorting states by what they can do
nodes.statement: A task splits states into useful and useless ones. Teleportation and key distillation draw lines that differ from distillability, and from each other.

nodes.label: Teleportation fidelity
nodes.title: Teleportation fidelity is fixed by singlet fraction
nodes.statement: Best teleportation fidelity is directly tied to the maximal singlet fraction attainable by trace-preserving LOCC, giving a task-based threshold on states.

nodes.label: Teleportation implies nonlocal
nodes.title: States useful for teleportation are nonlocal resources
nodes.statement: Cavalcanti, Acín, Brunner and Vértesi show every entangled state useful for teleportation yields a Bell violation in a suitable scheme, linking the two classes.

nodes.label: All entanglement is a resource
nodes.title: Every entangled state can enhance teleportation of some state
nodes.statement: Masanes proved that any bipartite entangled state, even a bound one, can raise the teleportation power of some other state.

nodes.label: Key from bound entanglement
nodes.title: Bound entangled states can yield a secret key
nodes.statement: Horodecki, Horodecki, Horodecki and Oppenheim characterise states containing a private key and show key can be distilled from bound entangled states, so privacy draws a different line from distillability.

nodes.label: Which operations are free
nodes.title: Classification depends on the allowed operations
nodes.statement: Each class of free operations gives a different resource theory, with different equivalences and conversions. Enlarging the class often simplifies the mathematics, while raising the question of what physical meaning remains.

nodes.label: Resource theory framing
nodes.title: Entanglement is a resource theory of free states and operations
nodes.statement: Choosing the free states and free operations sets the rules, and comparing theories becomes a way to see which features depend on those rules.

nodes.label: LOCC: natural but intricate
nodes.title: LOCC is physically natural yet mathematically hard
nodes.statement: LOCC captures what separated labs can do, but its structure is complex enough that even characterising the class is difficult, which motivates the larger classes below.

nodes.label: Separable operations
nodes.title: Separable operations strictly contain LOCC
nodes.statement: Rains studied entanglement purification under separable superoperators. Nonlocality without entanglement shows orthogonal product states that LOCC cannot reliably distinguish, a task separable measurements manage.

nodes.label: PPT-preserving operations
nodes.title: PPT-preserving operations make many quantities computable
nodes.statement: Relaxing LOCC to operations that preserve the partial transpose's positivity turns many optimisations into semidefinite programs, and gives bounds for LOCC.

nodes.label: Distillation as an SDP
nodes.title: PPT distillation fidelity is a semidefinite program
nodes.statement: Rains shows the maximum fidelity of a PPT distillation protocol solves a semidefinite program. This gives new upper bounds on LOCC-distillable entanglement.

nodes.label: Cost tied to log-negativity
nodes.title: PPT entanglement cost is tied to logarithmic negativity
nodes.statement: Audenaert, Plenio and Eisert relate PPT cost directly to log-negativity, and show that cost and distillation coincide for the antisymmetric Werner state.

nodes.label: PPT is still irreversible
nodes.title: Entanglement is irreversible under PPT operations
nodes.statement: Wang and Duan resolved this question with a computable additive bound on the regularised relative entropy of entanglement, showing a gap between cost and distillation for some states.

nodes.label: Asymptotic reversibility
nodes.title: Under which operations is entanglement reversible?
nodes.statement: A second law of entanglement would mean one quantity decides all conversions. Whether this holds depends sharply on the free operations.

nodes.label: LOCC is irreversible
nodes.title: Entanglement manipulation under LOCC is irreversible
nodes.statement: Creating a bound entangled state costs entanglement, yet none can be recovered, so LOCC has no single entanglement currency for mixed states.

nodes.label: Non-entangling ops are reversible
nodes.title: Entanglement is reversible under all non-entangling operations
nodes.statement: False. Lami and Regula showed that entanglement theory stays irreversible even under all non-entangling transformations.

nodes.label: Generalised Stein's lemma
nodes.title: Reversibility under asymptotically non-entangling operations
nodes.statement: Once operations may generate vanishing entanglement, reversibility holds with the regularised relative entropy as the single quantity. The proof rests on the generalised quantum Stein's lemma, whose original proof had a gap repaired in 2024.

nodes.label: States as channels
nodes.title: The Choi correspondence reads states as channels
nodes.statement: Bipartite states and channels are two views of the same object, so classifications of one carry over to the other.

nodes.label: Entanglement-breaking channels
nodes.title: Separable Choi states correspond to entanglement-breaking channels
nodes.statement: A channel destroys all entanglement with a reference exactly when its Choi state is separable.

nodes.label: PPT² conjecture
nodes.title: Is the composition of two PPT maps always entanglement breaking?
nodes.statement: Equivalently, can entanglement swapping across two PPT links ever produce entanglement? The conjecture says it cannot.
nodes.unknown: It has been proved in dimension 3 and for Gaussian channels. Higher finite dimensions remain open.

nodes.label: Measures
nodes.title: Ordering states by quantity
nodes.statement: Measures replace classes with numbers. For mixed states they split by construction, and they disagree about which state has more.

nodes.label: Axioms and extreme measures
nodes.title: Measures are bracketed by distillation and formation
nodes.statement: A quantity qualifies as a measure by not increasing under LOCC. Any measure suited to the regime of many pairs lies between distillable entanglement and entanglement of formation.

nodes.label: Measures order states differently
nodes.title: Different measures can disagree on which state is more entangled
nodes.statement: Eisert and Plenio compared measures directly. Virmani and Plenio showed that any two good asymptotic measures are either identical or order some states differently.

nodes.label: Convex-roof measures
nodes.title: Measures built from pure-state decompositions
nodes.statement: Extend a pure state measure to mixed states by taking the cheapest decomposition. These are physically direct but generally hard to compute.

nodes.label: Entanglement of formation
nodes.title: Entanglement of formation has a two-qubit closed form
nodes.statement: Wootters, building on Hill and Wootters, gave an explicit formula for any two-qubit state. Beyond this, computing it generally needs optimisation.

nodes.label: Concurrence
nodes.title: Concurrence extends to arbitrary dimensions
nodes.statement: Introduced for two qubits by Hill and Wootters, concurrence was generalised to higher dimensions through universal state inversion by Rungta and coauthors.

nodes.label: Geometric measure
nodes.title: Geometric measure: overlap with the nearest product state
nodes.statement: On pure states this measure uses the largest overlap with a product state, and extends to mixed states by a convex roof. Barnum and Linden studied related monotones.

nodes.label: Formation is additive
nodes.title: Entanglement of formation is additive
nodes.statement: False. Shor tied this to other additivity questions, and Hastings's counterexample settled all of them, so one-copy formation does not give the cost.

nodes.label: Cost: regularised formation
nodes.title: Entanglement cost is regularised entanglement of formation
nodes.statement: The asymptotic preparation cost equals the many-copy limit of formation, which is exact but hard to evaluate.

nodes.label: Distance-based measures
nodes.title: Measures of distance to the separable set
nodes.statement: Measure how far a state lies from separable states, or how much noise it takes to reach them.

nodes.label: Relative entropy of entanglement
nodes.title: Relative entropy measures distinguishability from separable states
nodes.statement: Vedral and coauthors proposed distance-based measures, of which relative entropy is central. Its regularisation is the quantity in the generalised Stein's lemma.

nodes.label: Relative entropy is additive
nodes.title: Relative entropy of entanglement is additive
nodes.statement: False. Vollbrecht and Werner gave a counterexample, which is why asymptotic theorems use the regularised version.

nodes.label: Robustness
nodes.title: Robustness measures the noise needed to remove entanglement
nodes.statement: Vidal and Tarrach define it as the minimal mixing with locally prepared states that washes out all entanglement.

nodes.label: One-shot rates
nodes.title: Smoothed distance measures give one-shot rates
nodes.statement: Brandão and Datta derive one-shot conversion rates under non-entangling maps from a smoothed max-relative entropy, and Buscemi and Datta study entanglement cost in a similar setting.

nodes.label: Operational and computable
nodes.title: Measures defined by tasks or by what can be calculated
nodes.statement: Some measures come from a task, while others are chosen because they can be evaluated or have useful properties. Rarely is a measure all three.

nodes.label: Negativity
nodes.title: Negativity and log-negativity can be computed for any state
nodes.statement: These come directly from the partial transpose. Log-negativity is a monotone despite not being convex. Being zero on all PPT states, neither sees bound entanglement.

nodes.label: Squashed entanglement
nodes.title: Squashed entanglement is additive and faithful
nodes.statement: Built from conditional mutual information minimised over extensions, it is additive and is strictly positive on all entangled states.

nodes.label: Formula for distillable entanglement?
nodes.title: Can distillable entanglement be computed in general?
nodes.statement: The one-way rate has a coding theorem, but it is a regularised optimisation over many copies.
nodes.unknown: Single-letter formulas are known only in special classes, with new non-degradable families added in 2026. No general tractable formula is known.

nodes.label: Families solved exactly
nodes.title: Where the classification can be completed
nodes.statement: Structure and symmetry make some families fully solvable. They are the test beds for every general conjecture on this page.

nodes.label: Two qubits
nodes.title: Two qubits are classified completely
nodes.statement: PPT decides separability, every entangled state is distillable, and formation has a closed form. Here the main classifications agree.

nodes.label: Werner and isotropic states
nodes.title: Twirling reduces states to one-parameter symmetric families
nodes.statement: Averaging over U⊗U gives Werner states and over U⊗U* gives isotropic states, each with one parameter. Their symmetry makes measures and distillation calculations far simpler.

nodes.label: Stabilizer states
nodes.title: Bipartite stabilizer states reduce to EPR pairs
nodes.statement: Local unitaries reduce any bipartite stabilizer state to EPR pairs and local states, so the pair count fully sets its entanglement.

nodes.label: Gaussian states
nodes.title: Gaussian states are classified by covariance matrices
nodes.statement: For Gaussian states of continuous-variable systems, separability and distillability reduce to conditions on a finite covariance matrix.

nodes.label: 1×N modes: PPT decides
nodes.title: PPT decides separability for 1×N mode Gaussian states
nodes.statement: Simon and Duan and coauthors gave two-mode criteria. Werner and Wolf extended the PPT result to one mode against any number of modes.

nodes.label: 2×2 modes: bound exists
nodes.title: Bound entangled Gaussian states exist in 2×2 modes
nodes.statement: With two modes on each side, Werner and Wolf give a family of explicit counterexamples: PPT no longer implies separable.

nodes.label: Complete covariance criterion
nodes.title: A computable criterion decides separability for all Gaussian states
nodes.statement: Giedke and coauthors give a necessary and sufficient, operational test for any number of modes. It is independent of partial transposition and strictly stronger.

nodes.label: Two-mode states all distil
nodes.title: All inseparable two-mode Gaussian states are distillable
nodes.statement: Giedke, Duan, Cirac and Zoller show that every entangled Gaussian state of two infinite-dimensional systems can be distilled. Their protocol includes a non-Gaussian step, a measurement of total particle number.

nodes.label: Gaussian ops can't distil
nodes.title: Gaussian operations alone cannot distil Gaussian states
nodes.statement: Giedke and Cirac characterise Gaussian operations and show they cannot distil Gaussian states. Eisert, Scheel and Plenio rule out the corresponding two-copy iterative protocols, so distillation needs a non-Gaussian step.

nodes.label: How entanglement scales
nodes.title: Sorting many-body states by how entanglement grows
nodes.statement: For a large system, the class of a state is how entanglement across a cut grows with the region. This classifies states by physics and by how hard they are to simulate.

nodes.label: Area law in 1D
nodes.title: Gapped 1D ground states obey an area law
nodes.statement: Hastings proved that ground states of gapped one-dimensional Hamiltonians have block entropy bounded by a constant, independent of block size.

nodes.label: Area law in 2D
nodes.title: Do gapped 2D ground states obey an area law?
nodes.statement: Anshu, Arad and Gosset prove an area law for locally gapped frustration-free 2D spin systems, with respect to a vertical bipartition of the lattice.
nodes.unknown: The result does not yet cover general gapped two-dimensional ground states or arbitrary regions.

nodes.label: Critical 1D: logarithmic
nodes.title: Critical 1D systems have logarithmic corrections
nodes.statement: Calabrese and Cardy show that entanglement entropy in 1+1-dimensional conformal field theories grows logarithmically with interval length, with a coefficient set by the central charge.

nodes.label: Random states: volume law
nodes.title: Random pure states are nearly maximally entangled
nodes.statement: Page computed the average subsystem entropy of a random pure state, which is close to maximal. Hayden, Leung and Winter show this concentrates sharply, and that large subspaces contain only almost maximally entangled states.

nodes.label: Topological entropy
nodes.title: A constant correction detects topological order
nodes.statement: Kitaev and Preskill, and Levin and Wen, independently extract a universal constant from the entropy of a region, which detects topological order in a ground state.

nodes.label: Entanglement spectrum
nodes.title: The entanglement spectrum holds more than entropy
nodes.statement: Li and Haldane propose the full spectrum of the reduced state as a generalisation of entropy, one that can identify topological order.

nodes.label: Entanglement and simulation
nodes.title: Limited entanglement allows efficient classical simulation
nodes.statement: Vidal shows that low Schmidt rank across cuts allows efficient simulation. Schuch and coauthors show even a von Neumann area law is not enough for matrix product state approximation, so Rényi entropies matter.
